evidence: observed_local = worker-equivalent Semgrep 1.168.0 run (served org ruleset + 41 default registry packs + worker excludes/excluded rules). NOT a Dashboard or CLI scan; findingfold/dedupe not applied.
line_convention: line = marker line (sink). A finding counts as on-line when its range covers it; case_span = enclosing handler/function.

cases.notes: User input only as an argument, via a parameter.
Literal format with argv[1] as an argument (the shape seen in tigergate-test-c).
argv copied to a buffer, printed via a literal %s.
Fixed server file. Classified candidate (not confirmed): safe only if that file is not attacker-writable.
Fixed command with no user input.
User-chosen file written to the response (path traversal; XSS depends on content).
Query value in an HTML response.
SSRF body copied into a text/html response.
getParameter used only for a boolean; nothing is written.
Stored in session; not rendered here.
Incomplete escaping in a quoted attribute.
Internal task name concatenated into the console.log format argument.
Internal count concatenated before a %d placeholder.
Username with newline forges log lines.
User input breaks JSON log structure.
Copied from path-traversal SAFE-004: allowlisted server file.
Copied from SAFE-006: resolve + relative containment.
Copied from SAFE-013: strict filename regex.
File read from a user-chosen path then sent. The real bug is path traversal; XSS depends on whether an attacker controls the file's content and the response type.
Same as FP-XSS-JS-001 via fs.readFile callback.
execSync(user command) output sent. Command injection is real; the attacker controls the command, so HTML in the output is plausible.
execFileSync with an argument array: output is git log text; attacker influence is limited to a path filter.
shelljs exec output sent; command string includes user input.
req.body reflected in an explicit text/html response.
Stored XSS: user-uploaded HTML served as text/html. The path is validated; the content is attacker-controlled.
User input echoed by a command and returned as HTML.
SSRF: attacker-chosen URL's body returned as HTML.
DOMXPath::query is XPath, not SQL. Genuine injection, wrong class.

observed_local.outcome: MISSED (only the SQLi rule fired: wrong class)

cases.notes: shell_exec output echoed; command injection is the primary bug, and the attacker can shape the output.
file_get_contents(user URL) echoed: attacker-controlled content (also SSRF/LFI).
float() in a numeric comparison; nan/inf can only cause a SQL error, not injection.
Raw string in an f-string query.
Database username: often user-chosen, so stored XSS is plausible; not provably safe.
